To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

genomic instability and bystanders are two distinct phenomena, both of which are initiated by radiation‐induced damage, and that bystander‐induced genomic instability can occur in both irradiated cells and bystander cells.

the induction of genomic instability and bystanders is dependent upon a common mechanism, which is the induction of DNA damage, but that these two phenomena are distinct in their induction, manifestation and biological outcomes.

(1) the induction of genomic instability and bystanders is not dependent on the induction of a specific DNA damage response; (2) genomic instability is induced in bystander cells, and this effect is not dependent on gap junctional communication; (3) bystander cells can induce genomic instability in irradiated cells, and (4) bystander cells are not dependent on gap‐junctional communication for their induction of genomic instability in irradiating cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
tracking genomic instability within irradiation‐induced bystander populations and the relationship between this and the bystander response.

elucidating the molecular mechanisms of radiation‐induced genomic instability, with the ultimate aim of identifying the molecular targets of radiation‐induce damage that may contribute to the induction of this complex response.
elucidating the relationship between genomic instability, bystander effects, and damage induction in mammalian cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a strong link between irradiated and bystanded populations, and that genomic instability is an important component of this relationship.
we are still a long way from understanding these responses and that the relationship between them remains a major area of interest and investigation.
the relationship between genomic instability, bystander effects and radiation‐induced DNA damage remains an open question.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are able to detect a significant number of radiation‐induced DNA double‐strand breaks (DSBs) in the irradiated cell, and that these DSBs are sufficient for the induction of both genomic instability and bystanders effects in the non‐irradiated cells.

genomic instability and bystanders are both manifestations of the same underlying cellular response to DNA damage and that the induction of genomic instability in bystanders is a consequence of a bystander‐mediated response.

we have developed a novel approach for tracking the fate of individual irradiated and bystanded cells over time and that we have used it to demonstrate that the bystander response is a direct consequence of the irradiated response and that the bystander and irradiated responses are not independent.
The main takeaway from our work is that

genomic instability is a complex response to radiation exposure that is not simply a function of the amount of damage induced, but rather is influenced by many other factors, both intrinsic and extrinsic to the irradiated cell.

genomic instability can be observed in both irradiated populations and bystander populations, but that the nature of the instability is different in the two populations and is likely to reflect different mechanisms of induction.
the relationship between genomic instability in irradiated cells and bystander effects may be more complex than previously thought.
